groups.title: Docker containers and the image layer model
groups.question: Your Node API's Docker image is over a gigabyte and rebuilds every dependency on every code change. Explain how images are built and how you would make them small and fast to build.

followUps.Images, containers, and the union filesy: What is the difference between an image and a container, and why do layers matter?
followUps.Multi-stage Dockerfiles for lean product: How does a multi-stage Dockerfile make the final image smaller?

evidence.text: An image is a stack of read-only filesystem layers.
A container is a running instance of an image with a thin writable layer on top.
Images that share base layers store and download them only once.

notEnough: Only saying a container is a running image.

evidence.text: A build stage installs dev dependencies and compiles the code.
The final stage copies only the built output and production dependencies.
Build tools and dev dependencies never reach the final image, so it is much smaller and safer.

notEnough: Only saying multi-stage builds are smaller.

groups.title: Docker Compose and multi-service networking
groups.question: You run your API and PostgreSQL together with Docker Compose, and after restarting, all your data is gone. Explain how Compose services find each other and how to keep data.

followUps.Docker Compose service discovery via con: How does the API connect to Postgres without knowing its IP address?
followUps.Named volumes for persistent PostgreSQL: Why did the database data disappear, and how do named volumes fix it?

evidence.text: Compose puts services on a shared network.
Each service can be reached by its service name, like postgres.
That name resolves to the right container, so no IP addresses are hard-coded.

notEnough: Only saying containers can talk to each other.

misconceptions.text: Says the API should connect to the database on localhost inside its container.

evidence.text: Data written inside a container is lost when the container is removed.
A named volume stores the data outside the container's lifecycle.
The database keeps its data across container restarts and recreation.

groups.title: Writing a Dockerfile for a Node/Express app
groups.question: You are writing the Dockerfile for your Express app, and the build is slow and somehow includes your .env file. Explain how you would order the instructions and what you would exclude.

followUps.Dockerfile instruction order: COPY packa: Why copy package.json and install dependencies before copying the source code?

evidence.text: Docker caches each instruction's layer and reuses it if its inputs did not change.
Copying package files and installing first means that layer is reused when only source code changes.
Only the later steps rerun, making rebuilds much faster.
It keeps files like node_modules, .env and .git out of the build context.
A smaller build context makes builds faster.
It stops secrets from ending up inside the image.

groups.title: Docker Compose for local full-stack development
groups.question: When you start your stack with Docker Compose, the API crashes because Postgres is not ready yet, and you need to inspect the database. Explain the day-to-day commands and how to order startup.

followUps.docker compose up, down, logs, and exec: Which Compose commands would you use to run, inspect and debug the stack?
followUps.Health checks and depends_on for service: Why isn't depends_on alone enough to make the API wait for Postgres?

evidence.text: up starts the services, optionally in the background, and down stops and removes them.
logs shows a service's output, and can follow it live.
exec runs a command inside a running container, such as opening a database shell.

notEnough: Only listing commands without what they do.

evidence.text: depends_on alone only waits for the container to start, not for the database to accept connections.
A health check tests whether Postgres is actually ready.
depends_on with the service_healthy condition makes the API wait until the health check passes.
